For anyone who wants to know, dead air is what really provides insulation for all these jackets. Dead air is the best insulator known to man outside of a vacuum. So the strands of wool, plastic, or down actually conduct heat significantly more than the air between the strands. The issue with using air as an insulator is that if the air gap gets too big, it allows convection to occur, and it is no longer insulating. This is where the materials (wool, down, etc.) come in, breaking up that gap to create multiple smaller gaps of dead air within the same volume. So even though down isn't nearly as good of an insulator than dead air, having it in the insulation allows for a larger gap to exist while still maintaining the properties of dead air. This leads to why higher fill power down is more insulating than lower fill (11:00). Lower fill down needs more down to maintain the same volume of dead air, which means there is more heat conducting material, making is less insulating. The higher fill down creates more amount of dead air while minimizing the amount of conduction going on in the insulation.  

I hope this makes sense.

It is true that the GoreTex patent has expired and that 3rd parties are using the same technology as Gore now,  but it is actually the opposite of what you would expect.  
Neither Gore nor 3rd parties have been using the old GoreText tech since before the patent has expired.  

The original GoreTex was very waterproof, but had poor breathability even while dry. The tech everyone is using now is slightly less waterproof, but far more breathable, so Gore also switched to that and has simply kept the GoreTex brand, since it was far too valuable to change.

One thing people seem to never mention: oversized == warmth. Restrictive clothing == cold. Too many layers == cold.

I have a completely different approach, and i'ts easy to try it out.

1) get a warm oversized down jacket. Not a lightweight layer but a nice warm jacket. If you are usually size M, get an L. If you're L, get an XL. Make sure it is long enough for the arms and waiste. Make sure it blocks some wind.
 Use a nice baselayer that's non-restrictive (can be a merino base or even a normal cotton tshirt just don't get those tight to skin base layers they're meant for activity). Then skip the mid layer and just wear the big down jacket. 

Your body heat will warm the air that's trapped inside the jacket. Honestly try it, it's often warmer to me than adding a midlayer. It's a bit complex to go into the why, but it's akin to sleeping without clothes is often warmer than sleeping with clothes provided you have a good sleeping bag.
You won't get sweaty because this generous air layer moves and breathes as you walk. So isntead of the moist air needing to evaporate through the jacket, it gets pushed out whilst you walk and new air enters the layer.

For down, its warmth is directly proportional to the loft (thickness) of the down. A puffier jacket will be warmer than a sleek thin one. The fill power is an inverse measurement of how much down you need to achieve a certain loft, so a 1000 fill power jacket  will have LESS down than a 650 fill power jacket with the same loft. These jackets will also be the same warmth (assuming same loft). I have many down jackets (I am both a backpacker and into heritage clothing) and love them for their lighweight feel and warmth/weight ratio, but also love heavy canvas jackets and waxed, wool lined jackets. Different clothes for different activities!

For a truly budget option I recommend checking out Legendary Whitetails Tough as Buck jacket. Dressy enough to be worn with a suit, rugged enough to be worn hunting. I own three of them in different colors. One I got for under $50! They are often on sale.

A big part of it is being cold makes you less cold. In that with enough controlled cold experiences, your body adapts. Over multiple years I have spent lots of time outdoors in the winter. I now spend most of winter in Chicago with jeans, a cotton t-shirt, wool flannel, wool hat, and a ski jacket. Most of the time I don't even use the hat or zip up the jacket, because my body just pumps blood faster and burns more calories to stay warm now. Only when polar vortices happen and it becomes truly arctic do I start wearing my merino wool base layers and add a scarf and hat and the like. 

Oh, and double sock your feet, one thin layer of merino wool and one thick layer of anything thick and fluffy that traps air (merino wool again for me). Even with cold adaptation, your feet will get cold if not actively using them. I find I don't need to wear insulated boots with good socks, unless I'm going to be sitting or standing outdoors for hours in the cold.

I live in Finland so it is very cold during some winters and out of curiosity I started looking for a winter jacket this fall. I fell down a rabbit hole to say the least. The most important deciding factor for choosing a jacket type is definitely the activity you are planning on doing. For city use pretty much anything works. Things get interesting if you have a specific activity in mind like hiking, climbing or whatever. Generally you want to use base-, mid-, and wind-layers during activity like hiking with a heavy backpack. After stopping get the extremely warm winter jacket over everything to keep body temperature up, this is often called a belay jacket or an expedition jacket. Btw a nylon wind layer over the base layer is very useful because it stops moisture (sweat) wicking into the belay jacket, keeping the down dry. Now this is where you have to make choises on the type of jacket. If you value durability you can go with wool, syntethic insulation or maybe even down with a very durable face fabric. If you value packability and low weight go with down with a low denier face fabric but watch out for pointy branches and sparks from the campfire. I found some spreadsheets from reddit that estimate the warmth of down jackets with an equation that takes into account the fill power and fill weight of down in jackets and calculates a warmth score for these. It isn't perfect but still a pretty cool comparison. For the whole layering system I recommend looking up how the US military does things (PCU and ECWCS systems). Those systems are originally from mountaineering and I feel like a lot of modern winter clothes are derived from there. After all this I decided that my current winter jacket was good enough and instead bought baselayers and a Patagonia Houdini for the wind layer.

If your base layer is cotton or (even better) linen, it will wick moisture, be breathable, and not have the problems of plastic. Linen is better than cotton for the purpose because the smelly bacteria doesn't settle there.

I ride my motorcycle through winter in Canada. I only wear old organic clothes that I thrifted. Nobody quite understands the mindset.. you have to dissociate. It's just going to suck, but it's temporary. It's like a cold shower or polar bear plunge, you can't make it enjoyable, and that's not the point. 

 Whatever speed you're going, add that to the wind chill on your whole body. Wind goes through the seams in $500 gloves and boots. It blasts through the zipper in the center of your coat and rught through your puffer jacket underneath.

I started because I couldn't afford a car, and thought investing in snowmobile gear would help. I was still cold, but the tiny bit if warmth I retained was torture. It was better to just accept being cold and adjust my mindset.

I dress like a voyageur in leather and fur.
Base layer of course.

Leather motorcycle jacket with a diagonal seam, the good vintage ones will have a lapel that you fold over the zipper and snap to your shoulder, which hides the zipper. 

A fur coat overtop. The fur, as the Eskimo learned, somehow diverts wind up and around you. Don't know how it works, but it works. 

Thin viscose or silk scarf around neck against your skin, thicker wool or fur pelt Overton to make the wind go around. Forms a seal with helmet, prevents wind going down your shirt.

Basic thermal underwear, leather pants, wool legwarmers at the calf to form a better seal at your ankles. Trenchcoat draped over thighs. Fishnet tights. The Finnish army wear fishnet bodysuit for warmth. Underneath wool socks, the friction of the fishnets creates warmth when you move and leaves small air pockets for warmth, preventing the wool overtop from clinging directly to your skin when you sweat. Leather boots with a little attachment I made like the old horseback riders had, not sure what they're called.. it's a flap that goes over your laces to prevent wind going straight through the shoe.

Gloves are a nightmare I've tried everything. Best has been thin leather gloves with a cotton lining, under XL disposable plastic gloves, under a snowmobile mitt.  Hands smell weird after, but the wind blasts through the most expensive mitts I can find. Heated gear but mitts especially, rated to work for hours and hours, doesn't feel like it helps much and then dies in 40 minutes because the batteries aren't insulated and the cold ruins them. If you have a ways to go when the heating cuts out, suddenly you experience the temperature drop and it's a worse feeling 20 minutes than if you had just ridden the full hour naked.
